# 2 Maccabees Chapter 3 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 3 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_003_page_001.jpg

---

**1** While the holy city was at complete peace and the laws were being upheld very well because of the piety of Onias the high priest and his hatred of wickedness,

**2** it came about that the kings themselves honored the place and glorified the temple with magnificent gifts.

**3** Seleucus, king of Asia, defrayed from his own revenues all the expenses connected with the service of the sacrifices.

**4** But a man named Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin, who had been appointed administrator of the temple, had a dispute with the high priest about the regulation of the city market.

**5** When he was unable to prevail over Onias, he went to Apollonius son of Thraseas, who at that time was governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia,

**6** and reported that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of untold sums of money — sums so large that the total could not be counted — and that these funds did not belong to the account of the sacrifices but could fall under the power of the king.

**7** When Apollonius met with the king, he informed him of the money that had been reported to him. The king chose Heliodorus, his chief minister, and sent him with instructions to remove the aforesaid funds.

**8** Heliodorus set out at once, using as his cover a tour of inspection through the cities of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, but actually intending to carry out the king's design.

**9** When he arrived in Jerusalem and had been received with courtesy by the high priest of the city, he told him what had been reported and made known the purpose of his visit, and he asked whether these things were in fact so.

**10** The high priest explained that these were deposits belonging to widows and orphans,

**11** and also some funds belonging to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, a man of very high standing; the total came to four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. He declared that it was utterly impossible to treat with injustice the people who had trusted in the holiness of the place and the dignity and inviolability of the temple that is honored throughout the whole world.

**12** But Heliodorus, because of the king's orders, insisted that the money must in any case be confiscated for the royal treasury.

**13** On the day appointed, he went in to conduct the inspection of these funds. There was no small distress throughout the whole city.

**14** The priests prostrated themselves before the altar in their priestly vestments and called toward heaven upon him who had given the law about deposits, that he should keep these funds safe for those who had entrusted them.

**15** To see the appearance of the high priest was itself to be wounded at heart, for his face and the change of his color revealed the anguish of his soul.

**16** Terror and a trembling of the body had come over the man, which made plain to those who looked at him the pain lodged in his heart.

**17** People rushed out from their houses in crowds to make a public supplication, because the holy place was about to be brought into dishonor.

**18** Women girded with sackcloth under their breasts thronged the streets. Young women who were kept indoors ran together — some to the gates, some to the walls, and others peered out of the windows.

**19** All of them stretched their hands toward heaven in supplication.

**20** There was something pitiable in the prostration of the whole multitude and in the anguish of the high priest as he endured such great distress.

**21** While they were calling upon the almighty LORD to keep safe what had been entrusted in full safety for those who had entrusted it, Heliodorus proceeded with his purpose.

**22** But just as Heliodorus arrived at the treasury with his bodyguard, the Sovereign of spirits and of all authority caused so great a manifestation that all who had dared to accompany him were struck down by the power of God and became faint with terror.

**23** For there appeared to them a horse with a terrifying rider, magnificently caparisoned. It rushed forward violently and struck Heliodorus with its front hooves. The rider appeared to be clothed in golden armor.

**24** Two young men also appeared, exceedingly strong and surpassingly handsome, gloriously beautiful in appearance. They stood on either side of Heliodorus and flogged him continuously, each inflicting many blows.

**25** Heliodorus fell suddenly to the ground, overwhelmed by great darkness. His men picked him up and placed him on a stretcher,

**26** and carried him away — this man who had entered the treasury just moments before with a great bodyguard and all his retinue, but who was now helpless to help himself. They acknowledged clearly the sovereign power of God.

**27** While he lay prostrate, speechless from the divine intervention and without any hope of recovery,

**28** they praised the LORD who had acted so marvelously for his own holy place. And the temple, which had been filled with fear and disturbance a little while before, was now filled with joy and gladness, since the almighty LORD had appeared.

**29** Some of Heliodorus's companions quickly besought Onias to call upon the Most High to grant life to the one who was lying at the very point of death.

**30** The high priest, fearing that the king might suspect some foul play on the part of the Jews in the case of Heliodorus, offered a sacrifice for the man's recovery.

**31** While the high priest was making the propitiatory sacrifice, the same young men again appeared to Heliodorus dressed in the same garments, and they stood and said, "Give great thanks to the high priest Onias, since it is for his sake that the LORD has granted you your life.

**32** And you yourself, having been scourged from heaven, proclaim to all people the majestic power of God." Having said this, they disappeared.

**33** Then Heliodorus offered sacrifice to the LORD and made very great vows to the Savior of his life, and bidding Onias farewell he marched back with his forces to the king.

**34** He bore testimony before all people to the works of the supreme God that he had seen with his own eyes.

**35** When the king asked Heliodorus what sort of person would be suitable to send to Jerusalem once more, he said,

**36** "If you have any enemy or any plotter against the government, send him there and you will receive him back thoroughly flogged — if indeed he survives — for there is assuredly some divine power at work in that place.

**37** For he who has his dwelling in heaven watches over that place and helps it, and he strikes down and destroys those who come to do it harm."

**38** So the affairs concerning Heliodorus and the preservation of the treasury had this ending.
